note: The most cited general LLM survey, covers pre-training, post-training, utilisation and evaluation in one frame.
title: A Survey of Large Language Models

reading.body:
With 4,657 citations, this is the most cited general survey of language models, covering pre-training, post-training, real-world use, and evaluation in a single framework.

Its citation count alone is data, a survey this widely cited has become a shared reference point that later, more specific papers build on and argue against, including several others in this collection. That makes it less a single research finding and more a map of the field as it stood in 2023, which is worth reading against the papers that followed and complicated parts of that map, such as the reasoning-collapse and unfaithful chain-of-thought findings elsewhere in this set.

As a survey rather than original research, it does not report new experimental results, and being published in 2023 it predates the reasoning-model and diffusion-model developments covered by later papers here.

abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has driven a transformative shift in artificial intelligence (AI), reshaping both research paradigms and practical applications. Distinguished from their predecessors by unprecedented scale and advanced capabilities, LLMs necessitate new frameworks for understanding their development, behavior, and societal impact. This survey systematically reviews recent advancements in LLM techniques across four key dimensions: (1) pre-training methodologies, which establish core model capabilities through large-scale self-supervised training, architectural innovations, and data curation strategies; (2) post-training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, which adapt foundational models to downstream tasks and enhance their alignment and safety; (3) utilization strategies, such as in-context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic reasoning, that optimize real-world deployment and enable effective interaction with external environments; and (4) evaluation methods, encompassing benchmarks for key ability dimensions such as core language capabilities, reasoning, and safety, which support comprehensive and reliable assessment of model performance. Additionally, we identify critical research issues, including those concerning theoretical foundations, efficient scaling, alignment, and agentic capability, and highlight the open challenges they present.
explain_beginner: If you wanted one long reading list to understand how something like ChatGPT is actually built, this is it. A large language model is the technology, trained on huge amounts of text, that lets a computer generate humanlike writing and answer questions. This survey, one of the most cited papers in the entire field, walks through the whole pipeline, how these systems learn from raw text in the first place, how they get fine tuned afterward to follow instructions and stay safer, how people actually use them day to day through prompting and step by step reasoning, and how researchers test whether they work at all. It does not report new experiments of its own, it organizes and explains what hundreds of other papers found, and the authors are candid that basic questions like why scaling up model size improves performance are still not theoretically well understood.
explain_business: This survey is most useful to an executive as a map of where competitive advantage in the LLM industry actually sits, because it separates building a competitive model into four distinct capability areas, acquiring and cleaning enough training data and compute, running the alignment and safety tuning that turns a raw model into something usable, building the application layer that turns model output into a product, and running the evaluation infrastructure that proves it works reliably. Few vendors are strong across all four, so this framing is directly useful for build versus buy decisions, since a company evaluating an AI vendor can ask which of these four stages that vendor actually controls versus buys in from someone else. It is a synthesis paper, not new research, so it carries no new regulatory or safety claims on its own, its value is organizing existing knowledge for faster onboarding into a fast moving field.
explain_practitioner: Zhao and colleagues organize the LLM literature into four stages, pre training, covering data curation, architecture choices, and self supervised objectives, post training, covering supervised fine tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback for alignment, utilization, covering in context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic tool use, and evaluation, covering benchmarks for language ability, reasoning, and safety. Because it is a synthesis rather than original experimental work, its evidentiary basis is the cited literature itself, and the authors have issued repeated revisions to keep pace with a field that moves faster than a single publication cycle. They flag open problems they consider unresolved rather than solved, the theoretical basis for why scale improves capability, how to make training and inference more computationally efficient, how to reliably align model behavior with human intent, and how to build genuinely agentic systems that plan and act reliably. Its main practitioner value is as a citation map into primary sources, not a standalone technical reference on its own.
